title: Odd idea that didn't work - why?

posts.topic_title: Odd idea that didn't work - why?
posts.author: eric343
posts.post_subject: Odd idea that didn't work - why?
posts.content_md:
I recently salvaged a Philips color-separating prism from an old LCD projector, and it turns out that it works as an excellent variable beamsplitter. (The ratio depends on the angle at which the light enters the prism.) As a result, I decided to try using it to improve the beam ratio in Denisyuks, having read that the optimal ratio is 1:3 to 1:1.5.

The configuration I tried was a modification of something I'd read about in the Holography Handbook; the reference beam hitting the plate as in a standard Denisyuk configuration, and the split-off beam diverged and illuminating the object from the side. Using a large first-surface mirror in the sand, I tried to get the reference beam to hit the plate at what I judged to be a 45-degree angle (up until now I'd simply been hitting it straight-on).

After setting it up, equalizing the path lengths, and checking the beam ratio with my handy S&M photometer, I let everything settle for awhile and made an exposure. Unfortunately, the only thing visible in the plate was a series of horizontal bands with an odd character to their bottom edge (not straight as would be expected from interference fringes). So I carded off the object beam and tried again -- still nothing. 

Now, I don't think that external vibration was a factor (my table is the sand tension table as described in the Holography Handbook and also in Saxby), and I let everything settle for about an hour. I'm wondering whether there's anything fundamentally wrong with this setup, or whether it's likely that I simply got the exposure way off. I don't *think* I massively underexposed it judging by the speed at which it developed... unfortunately, I haven't figured out how to translate the readings from the S&M meter into exposure times.

posts.post_subject: Odd idea that didn't work - why?
posts.content_md:
> **eric343:** Unfortunately, the only thing visible in the plate was a series of horizontal bands with an odd character to their bottom edge (not straight as would be expected from interference fringes).

Are the bands visible to the eye before you make the exposure? (If 'no', continue)

Are the bands consistant across the plate or the object?

If the plate, then the plate is moving during exposure.

If the object, then the object is moving.

It is likely you aren't settling long enough. Or, the temperatures of everything aren't the same. (You aren't pulling your plate right from the fridge, are you?).

I'm having similar issues, and I think my trouble is my plate holder isn't rigid enough.

-Phil

posts.author: eric343
posts.post_subject: Odd idea that didn't work - why?
posts.content_md:
The bands are consistent across the plate (there's no image of the object visible; the bands are only visible with the light at a very particular angle). For the record, I'm not using much of a plateholder -- it's a piece of Fimo clay that I stuck the edge of an old plate in and baked. The plate is effectively propped up on its edge.

I don't think the plateholder is at fault, though, as I've successfully made holograms with it before.

Temperature could be a problem, as the settling time after handling the plate is only about 45 seconds. (time to place the plate and then find my way over to the keypad / display that's hooked up to the BASIC stamp controlling the servo-operated shutter [which is suspended on a boom to keep the motor vibrations off the table], and then the programmed 30 second settling time of the BASIC stamp.

I doubt it though -- the plates are stored at room temperature, and my hands aren't that warm.

posts.topic_title: Odd idea that didn't work - why?
posts.author: JohnFP
posts.post_subject: Odd idea that didn't work - why?
posts.content_md: Eric if you has just loaded a plate and then it was 45 seconds till exposure, your effective settle time is only 45 seconds not 1 hour. In a Denisyk, plate movement to object is the main factor you want to elliminate. Let the plate settle for longer and what I have done before in stablizing a plate held from the bottom only is lay a long object of a couple of pounds across the top of the plate and to the table. I used a hunk of steel about 18 inches long and 3 inches wide. This keeps the top from moving to and fro.

posts.author: Bastian_S
posts.post_subject: Odd idea that didn't work - why?
posts.content_md:
hmm It could be your variable beamsplitter is a polarization dependant BS. 

So the polarization direction of 1 beam is different to the other beam by 90°. Perpendicularly polarized light doesnt interfere.

I guess the only thing you get are those newton rings from light being reflected in the glass of your holder.

If im guessing right youd need a half- waveplate to turn the polarization direction of 1 beam. but unless your lucky it shouldnt be easier to get than a proper variable BS

edit :

after re-reading your post im not sure if you have the kind of BS im thinking of.

Is a cube made of 2 triangular prisms and you modulate the ratios by turning your laser (=the polarization of the light)? If yes thats what Im thinking of. If no my guess is probably wrong.
